name: Dopamine detox

lead: A dopamine detox means pulling back from stimulating habits such as social media, gaming, junk food and pornography for a set period. In ascension circles it is used to regain focus and motivation so gym, grooming and study routines get done, sometimes alongside no-masturbation challenges.

It was popularised in 2019 by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a behavioural tool for compulsive habits, and he has said the name is misleading since the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not lower dopamine. Neuroscientists say dopamine drives motivation and learning and cannot be reset by avoiding stimuli. No large trials test it directly; related reviews of social-media detoxes report a small reduction in depressive symptoms.

paras: People set a period, from a day to a few weeks, in which they cut phones, social media, gaming, junk food or porn, and fill the time with exercise, reading or study. Some forum users report feeling focused afterward, while others report feeling flat.

Extreme versions may worsen anxiety, loneliness or restrictive habits, and the practice is not a treatment for addiction or depression. Some people describe withdrawal-like symptoms when quitting substances alongside it.

chain: Cut phones, porn and junk food
angle.text: Ascension circles use temporary abstinence from stimulating activities to regain motivation for gym, grooming and study routines. The idea that it resets brain chemistry is disputed by neuroscientists, and no appearance outcomes have been tested.

lead: A dopamine detox, also called dopamine fasting, is a wellness practice of temporarily stepping away from pleasurable or stimulating activities such as social media, gaming, junk food, shopping and pornography, with the aim of regaining focus, discipline and enjoyment of ordinary activities.[1][2] People pursuing self-improvement use it to free up time and attention for training, sleep, skincare routines and other habits that feed into how they look, and some also describe a calmer, more present demeanour afterwards. It was popularised in 2019 by California psychologist Cameron Sepah, who framed it as a cognitive behavioural tool for compulsive behaviours.[1][3]

Sepah has said the name is misleading and that the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not to lower dopamine itself; he is quoted calling dopamine a mechanism that explains how addictions become reinforced and 'a catchy title'.[1][3] Neuroscientists and health commentators have criticised the framing, noting that dopamine is involved in motivation, learning and reward prediction, while several commentators describe the underlying idea of scheduled breaks from cues as sensible.[1][3][4]

Research on the practice is indirect. No large randomised trials have tested dopamine fasting directly,[2] but meta-analyses of randomised trials of social media reduction report small improvements in depressive symptoms and in well-being.[5][6] On looksmax.org the idea appears in threads promoting it as a productivity or motivation reset, and in threads where users report disappointing results.[7][8]

paras: Definitions vary. Some versions limit the practice to online technology, while others extend it to work, exercise, conversation and physical contact; an extreme version is sensory deprivation.[1] Targets listed in coverage include smartphones, social media, emotional eating, gaming, gambling, shopping, and pornography or masturbation, and proponents often pair the break with reading, crafting or outdoor activity.[1]

Sepah's own framework, as summarised by Harvard Health, applies to six behaviours: emotional eating, excessive internet and gaming, gambling and shopping, pornography and masturbation, thrill-seeking and recreational drugs. It argues that tolerating boredom or loneliness can help people regain control of compulsive behaviours.[3]

sections.h: How it is used to improve looks
paras: In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, the stated benefit chain is behavioural: less scrolling and impulse eating frees time and energy, which people redirect to lifting, sleep, skincare, grooming and routines that affect appearance.[7] Some also describe a calmer, more present demeanour afterwards. Forum posters group it with 'motivationmaxxing' and no-masturbation challenges.[8]

Wikipedia credits Sepah with developing the practice and naming it, describing it as drawing on stimulus-control methods from CBT.[1] Media coverage in 2019 and 2020 described the idea as a Silicon Valley wellness trend.[1] Grokipedia states it spread through Silicon Valley circles, social media and productivity podcasts and peaked during the 2020 lockdowns.[2]

Wikipedia lists a run of 2019-2020 coverage: Vice (October 2019) called it a wellness trend with the headline 'Sounds Fake, but OK', Psych Central (November 2019) argued it probably does not work, and The New York Times (November 2019) reported a subject who found everyday life more exciting afterwards. Further commentary followed from a University of Reading neuroscientist, a University of Connecticut Q and A with behavioural neuroscientist John Salamone, The Conversation and the Harvard Health blog (February 2020), with explainers still appearing in 2024.[1] Wikipedia also lists Marie Claire (January 2020), Inc.com, Psychologies, Psychiatric Times and Maclean's coverage in 2024.[1]

Sepah's framework uses graduated fasts at daily, weekly, quarterly and yearly intervals, with limited periods of normal indulgence between them, and psychiatrist Anna Lembke has endorsed a 24-hour phone-free fast as a starting point, noting that a fuller reset may take three to four weeks or more.[2] Harvard Health describes the schedule as minimally disruptive: a few hours each evening, a weekend day, a weekend each quarter or a week each year.[3]

A looksmax.org post describes a seven-day reduction of social media, no phone in the bedroom and replacing stimulation with exercise, reading and sunlight, and says it is not about cutting out dopamine itself.[7] The same guide thread suggests, in its author's words, no extreme rules: limiting social media to 30 to 60 minutes a day, no phone in the bedroom, no screen in the first hour of the morning, and eating without a screen, then filling the time with exercise, reading, learning, goal work and sunlight.[7] This is a forum poster's protocol and has not been tested in trials.

Harvard Health's Peter Grinspoon wrote in February 2020 that the fast has little to do with fasting or dopamine, that dopamine does not fall when people avoid stimulating activities, and that periodic disconnection is worthwhile but not new, citing the Sabbath and meditation. He criticised followers who adopt versions that cut out eating, exercise or socialising.[3] Wikipedia quotes him describing Sepah's approach as sensible and criticising 'ever more extreme, ascetic, and unhealthy' versions.[1]

Neuroscientist Ciara McCabe of the University of Reading has called the idea that the brain can be reset by avoiding dopamine triggers 'nonsense'.[1] Neurologist Richard Cytowic wrote in Psychology Today in 2020 that dopamine is not a depletable stock that fasting can replenish and suggested a 'stimulation fast' aimed at specific cues instead.[4]

Wikipedia's article states that technology use raises dopamine by roughly 50 to 100 percent, compared with figures cited for drugs such as heroin, cocaine and amphetamine, and that it has not been conclusively shown that technology use makes the brain less responsive to dopamine; it also notes that freed time can go to habits such as exercise.[1]

A 2025 meta-analysis in Behavioral Sciences by Liu and colleagues pooled 20 randomised trials (10,106 participants, mostly college students, with interventions typically one to two weeks) and reported a small positive effect of social media detox on well-being (d about 0.23).[5] A 2025 meta-analysis by May, Malouff and Meynadier pooled 10 trials (1,491 participants) and reported a small reduction in depressive symptoms (g about 0.28), with limited-use interventions looking similar to full abstinence; the authors noted that none of the trials examined problematic users and that more high-quality studies are needed.[6]

Grokipedia describes an earlier 2024 meta-analysis of about 10 detox studies as finding a small reduction in depressive symptoms but no significant effects on life satisfaction, stress or overall well-being.[2] Wikipedia lists studies by Fei and colleagues (2022) on dopamine fasting as an intervention for behavioural addiction, Sussman and Weigle (2024) on dopamine detoxification for problematic gaming, and Zheng and colleagues (2024) associating more screen time with greater impulsivity in adults aged 30 to 45.[1]

Extreme versions may worsen anxiety, loneliness or restrictive patterns, and the practice is not a treatment for addiction or depression; people with ADHD or substance use disorders are advised to consult a professional first.[2] Harvard Health notes that some followers misread it as a 'tolerance break' and drop eating, exercise or social contact, which was not part of Sepah's original idea.[3] Wikipedia's NoFap article, on a related abstinence community, reports that a 2021 qualitative study linked commitment to abstinence with ongoing distress and that a 2023 preregistered survey associated NoFap practices with harm-causing effects.[9]

One looksmax.org user reported that a week of cutting out social media and music left everything feeling bland, and another replied that it is comparable to no-masturbation challenges.[8] The practice overlaps with NoFap, founded by Alexander Rhodes in June 2011, whose members report benefits that therapists and researchers say have little medical evidence behind them.[9]
Related ideas include digital detoxes, stimulus control from CBT, NoFap and other abstinence challenges, and Lembke's pleasure-pain balance framework.[2][9]

No studies found testing dopamine fasting itself. Related work on social media reduction is described above.[5][6][2] A 2018 review by Christopher Ferguson reported that technology use raises dopamine far less than drugs of abuse and found no conclusive evidence that it desensitises the brain.[1]
